sections.title: What a plumber invoice must show
sections.body: A professional plumbing invoice needs more than just a total amount. Customers want to see exactly what they are paying for. Start by clearly separating your materials from your time. If you charge a call-out fee or a minimum first-hour charge, list this as its own line item. Describe the work completed in plain language, such as 'repaired leaking kitchen trap' rather than just 'plumbing repair'. If the job requires a second visit because you had to order a specific part, note this clearly on the document so the customer understands the timeline and the billing structure.
items: Clear hourly or fixed labour rates

sections.title: How plumber work is usually priced
sections.body: Plumbing work usually falls into two categories: emergency repairs and planned installations. For repairs, most plumbers charge a call-out fee that covers the first hour, plus an hourly rate thereafter. Emergency out-of-hours work attracts a premium rate. For planned work like fitting a new bathroom, customers expect a fixed price. This is where providing a written quotation before starting is vital. Agreeing on the scope of work upfront prevents the most common disputes in this trade. You can easily draft these documents using our free invoice generator at /tools/free-invoice-generator without needing an account.

sections.title: Getting paid: terms, deposits and chasing
sections.body: Cash flow is critical when you are buying expensive materials like boilers and copper piping. For large jobs, always take a deposit to cover the cost of parts before you begin work. State your payment terms clearly on every invoice. Many domestic plumbers require payment upon completion, while commercial contractors might offer a thirty-day window. If a customer delays payment, send a polite but firm payment reminder. Having a clear paper trail from the initial quotation to the final invoice makes it much easier to chase late payments and protect your business income.

faqs.q: How do I invoice for a job that requires a second visit?
faqs.a: If you need to order a part and return later, you can either invoice for the initial call-out and labour immediately, or wait to issue a single invoice upon completion. Most plumbers prefer to wait and issue one final bill that includes the initial visit, the new part, and the second visit labour, ensuring the customer sees the complete picture.

faqs.q: Should I mark up the cost of plumbing parts?
faqs.a: Yes, it is standard practice to apply a markup to parts you supply. This covers your time spent sourcing, collecting, and guaranteeing the materials. You do not need to show the markup on the invoice. Simply list the final retail price you are charging the customer for the copper pipe, valves, or fixtures.

faqs.q: Why is a written quotation important for plumbing work?
faqs.a: A written quotation prevents disputes by setting clear expectations. When a customer agrees to a fixed price for a bathroom installation in writing, they cannot argue about the final cost unless the scope of work changes. It protects you from customers who underestimate the time and materials required for complex plumbing jobs.

faqs.q: How do I handle emergency call-out fees on the invoice?
faqs.a: List the emergency call-out fee as the very first line item on your invoice. This makes it clear that the premium charge is for the immediate response, separate from the actual repair work or parts used. Transparency here stops customers from questioning why a simple leak repair cost more at two in the morning.
